title.rendered: Palm Beach’s “Ham and Cheese House” finds buyer at $105M

content.rendered:
Palm Beach’s historic “Ham and Cheese” house found a buyer, with an asking price of $105 million, marking the county’s priciest contract of the season.

That’s one of the 16 luxury contracts Palm Beach County buyers signed from Oct. 19 to Oct. 25, according to Douglas Elliman’s Eklund Gomes Team, which tracks all residential listings over $3 million.

The contracts totaled $197.5 million in asking volume, marking the biggest buying week of the quarter. Buyers signed 12 contracts for single-family homes and four for condos.

Single-family contracts added up to $169.4 million in volume. They had an average asking price of $14.1 million, or $1,870 per square foot, and spent an average of 70 days on the market — though the historic Palm Beach home made up a majority of the asking volume and skewed the average upward.

Condo contracts totaled $28 million in asking volume, with an average price of $7 million, or $2,214 per square foot, and 157 days on the market. Among the contracts was a unit asking $9.7 million in the Related Group and BH Group’s Ritz-Carlton residences in West Palm Beach.

title.rendered: Fintech firm adds 175K sf to Flatiron District office

content.rendered:
A financial technology firm has ramped up its presence at a Flatiron District office building — again.

Ramp signed an expansion for 175,000 square feet of additional space at Williams Equities’ 28-40 West 23rd Street, the Commercial Observer reported. The length and asking rent of the expansion were not disclosed; the average asking rent for Class B office space in Midtown South was $80.85 per square foot in the third quarter, according to Colliers.

It’s the second time this year that Ramp grew at the building, and the third overall. Back in March, the company added 153,000 square feet to its footprint at the property. Ramp initially took 66,000 square feet from Microsoft in a 2023 sublease agreement before converting to a direct deal and doubling its space.

With the latest addition, Ramp’s total at the property is 460,000 square feet, a vast majority of the 575,000-square-foot complex.

CBRE’s Ryan Alexander, Jared Isaacson and Jeff Frenkel represented Ramp in the expansion, while Williams Equities principals Michael T. Cohen and Andrew Roos — who also work for Colliers — were among those representing the landlord.

title.rendered: Estates at Acqualina penthouse with private pool lands $40M contract

content.rendered:
A North Miami Beach penthouse topped Miami’s luxury market last week, landing a contract at an asking price of $40 million.

The pending sale is the priciest of the 15 contracts signed between Oct. 19 and Oct. 25, according to the weekly report by Douglas Elliman’s Eklund-Gomes team. The report tracks all listings in Miami-Dade asking $4 million and above.

The condos and single-family homes that went under contract last week spent an average of 244 days on the market. They had a combined asking price of $149.5 million, similar to the previous week, which recorded 13 contracts totaling $120.7 million. 

Of the deals that went under contract last week, 10 were for single-family homes. They spent an average of 260 days on the market and had a combined asking price of $85.5 million. The average contract price was $8.5 million, or $1,630 per square foot.

title.rendered: “They’re getting hammered”: Fisher Island Club fee dispute escalates into $5M class action after community association sues members

content.rendered:
A group of Fisher Island Club members are accusing the island’s community association of over charging non-property-owners.

The members are seeking a class action lawsuit, alleging the association improperly charged member fees to non-owners after the association sued two members in state court to collect the disputed charges.

Steven D. Richman, Stephen Courey and Mark Lorberbaum filed the class-action complaint against the Fisher Island Community Association Inc. on Oct. 22 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida over allegations that the association lacks the authority to impose the fees, known as non-property-owner fees. The lawsuit seeks refunds, a declaration that the charges are unenforceable, and an injunction against their continued imposition and collection.

The association “is taking advantage of club members, compelling them to pay these unlawful fees,” said The Kon Firm’s Joshua R. Kon, David Robbins and Zalman Margolin, the legal team representing the members in the federal case. “Rather than own its mistakes, [the association] has publicly threatened club members with suspension and expulsion from the island.”

title.rendered: LA City Council shoots down appeals, greenlights 814-unit Studio City project

content.rendered:
The Los Angeles City Council sided with developers of a planned mixed-use apartment complex in Studio City. 

The City Council upheld the approval of a proposal from a joint venture of Genton Property Group, RC Development and Torino Companies for Riverwalk at Studio City, a multifamily development boasting 814 units, Urbanize Los Angeles reported. 

The approval comes after several appeals from neighbors who sought to block construction of the mixed-use apartment complex. The development would replace existing commercial buildings at 12555 Ventura Boulevard with a series of two- to seven-story structures, 814 residences, as well as 76,000 square feet of commercial space and parking for more than 800 vehicles on four underground levels.

title.rendered: New York developer pitches Fort Lauderdale’s tallest tower at 645 feet

content.rendered:
Fort Lauderdale’s skyline could soon have a new king. 

New York-based NE 2nd Holdings, managed by Alexander Lichtman of Arosa Developers, has filed plans for what would be the tallest building in Fort Lauderdale, the South Florida Business Journal reported. 

The proposal for the 0.7-acre site at 117, 115 and 109 Northeast Second Street calls for a 1.1 million-square-foot tower rising 56 stories, or 645 feet. The tower would replace an existing parking lot and 4,000-square foot warehouse with 696 residential units, 7,400 square feet of commercial space and 696 parking spaces, the outlet said. 

The plan calls for 138 studios, 296 one-bedroom units, 218 two-bedrooms units, four two-bedrooms units with dens, 48 three-bedroom units and two three-bedroom units with dens. The floorplans would range from 554 to 1,170 square feet. Amenity decks with pools are planned for the 10th floor and the rooftop.

FMSY Architects + Planners is the architect. Fort Lauderdale-based Keith is the planning firm. 

Arosa Developers has the property under contract from the Mary T. Viator Trust and Westella LLC. Fort Lauderdale’s Development Review Committee will consider the plans for the site on Oct. 27.

title.rendered: Rockpoint lists downtown SF offices as investor interest in market heats up

content.rendered:
Rockpoint Group is seeking a buyer for an office building in downtown San Francisco. 

Rockpoint listed 100 Pine Street in the Financial District for sale, the San Francisco Business Times reported. The Boston-based real estate private equity firm acquired the property in 2017 for $287.5 million, or roughly $714 per square foot. Pricing guidance for the latest listing hasn’t been disclosed, though marketing materials pitch the building as available below replacement cost.

The 33-story building spans over 402,000 square feet and is about three-quarters occupied. JLL’s Rob Hielscher and Adam Lasoff hold the listing. 

The 100 Pine Street building opened in 1972, the same year as the Transamerica Pyramid. It once served as Continental Insurance’s headquarters, earning it the longtime name of the Continental Insurance Building.

In 2018, Rockpoint invested in a capital improvement program that upgraded the lobby and elevators, and renovated the outdoor plaza. It also overhauled the fifth-floor amenity center, adding a conference center, wellness area, showers and lockers.

title.rendered: Fortune, Château score $463M loan for St. Regis Sunny Isles

content.rendered:
Edgardo Defortuna’s Fortune International Group and the Grosskopf family’s Château Group secured a $463 million loan package for the St. Regis Residences, Sunny Isles Beach, marking one of the largest loans to close in the beachfront city. 

Madison Realty Capital is providing the financing, according to a news release. It refinances existing debt backing the two-tower luxury condo development at 18801 Collins Avenue, including loans provided by Bank OZK dating back to 2020. In April, the developers closed on $113.8 million in construction financing from City National Bank. 

New York-based Madison is led by managing principals Brian Shatz, Josh Zegen and Adam Tantleff.

Berkadia’s Scott Wadler, Michael Basinski, Mitch Sinberg and others arranged the latest loan and the City National financing, according to the release. Vertical construction of the south tower is underway, and the sales center was relocated across the street as the developers prepare to break ground on the north tower next. The debt will also be used to expand the food and beverage and hospitality amenities.

title.rendered: Developers snap up multifamily sites despite higher costs, overbuilding

content.rendered:
A pair of developers scooped up two separate multifamily project sites, as South Florida construction costs stay elevated and the region has barely emerged from years of oversupply in the rental market. 

In the bigger deal, an affiliate of Brickell-based North Development paid $32.8 million for the 0.6-acre lot on the northwest corner of North Bayshore Drive and Northeast 21st Street in Miami’s Edgewater, according to property records and real estate database Vizzda. The lot is immediately west of the Biscayne 21 condominium that was the subject of a protracted legal battle until recently between holdout unit owners and the firm planning to redevelop the building. 

North Development is a partnership between Ricardo Dunin’s Oak Capital and Peruvian development and fund management firm Edifica. North’s founding partners include Dunin, Juan Carlos Tassara, Eduardo Vargas, Arturo Vidal, Jorge Ruiz and Martin Bedoya. 

The seller was an entity that’s a partnership among Dallas-based Mill Creek Residential, TPG Equity REIT and UBS Realty Investors. The entity had paid $8 million for the property.

title.rendered: Driftwood, Merrimac, MV Real Estate score $145M loan for Miami Riverside Wharf mixed-use project

content.rendered:
The developers of the $350 million Riverside Wharf along the Miami River scored a nine-figure construction loan from a regional bank for the 200,000-square-foot mixed-use project.

Driftwood Capital, Merrimac Ventures and MV Real Estate Holdings secured $145 million in construction financing from Arkansas-based Centennial Bank to fund the vertical construction of the waterfront nine-story, two-tower project at 114 Southwest North River Drive, according to a news release.

Riverside Wharf will include a 167-room Dream Hotel, 30,000-square-foot nightclub, a rooftop pool and day club, a 12,000-square-foot event hall and 16,000 square feet of restaurant space, with completion targeted for fall 2028. The project was designed by Jon Cardello of CUBE 3 Architects, with Gensler handling construction documents and ICrave overseeing interior design.

Plans also call for the revival and expansion of Breakwater Hospitality Group’s The Wharf Miami, a public riverwalk, a new seawall and a pop-up location for Garcia’s Fish Market, a nod to the area’s fishing heritage.

Led by Emi Guerra and Alex Mantecon, Breakwater Hospitality operates the The Wharf Fort Lauderdale on the banks of the New River, JohnMartin’s in Coral Gables, Regatta Grove in Coconut Grove and PIER 5 at Bayside in downtown Miami, both along Biscayne Bay.

title.rendered: Jordan Kaplan backs Xavier Becerra’s run for California governor

content.rendered:
Another Southern California real estate backer of Matt Mahan has switched to Xavier Becerra. 

Douglas Emmett Chair and CEO Jordan Kaplan last week donated the one-time maximum of $39,200 to Becerra’s run for California governor, campaign finance records show. The Santa Monica-based REIT, which reports earnings next month, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 

Kaplan previously gave $78,400 to Mahan’s campaign for governor before the San Jose mayor — the favorite of L.A.’s real estate circle and Silicon Valley — failed to make it past the June primary despite his roster of wealthy backers. 

Billionaire mall magnate Rick Caruso pumped more than $1 million into Mahan’s campaign. Then he and others chose Becerra, a former Joe Biden cabinet member. That crew includes Kilroy CEO Angela Aman and Marcus & Millichap founder and chair George Marcus. Separately, Marcus spent $2 million to defeat the proposed billionaire tax, also on the November ballot and a measure Becerra has said he doesn’t support.

title.rendered: Roxborough Group buys Fremont apartments for $109M in latest East Bay multifamily sale

content.rendered:
Another multifamily property in the Bay Area has traded hands as investor confidence in the region grows. 

San Francisco-based real estate investment firm Roxborough Group acquired the Bidwell Park apartment complex at 39800 Fremont Boulevard in Fremont for $109.4 million, Mercury News reported. Pacific Urban Investors was the seller. 

The deal for the 246-unit property works out to $444,500 per unit. That’s about 65 percent higher than the average per-unit sales price for apartments in the East Bay of roughly $270,000, per Marcus & Millichap data cited by Mercury News. Portions of the East Bay multifamily market have attracted investor interest because of a dearth of new market-rate construction. 

“As a result of the limited construction pipeline and consistent renter demand, vacancy is expected to decline faster this year than in 2025,” Marcus & Millichap said in its report. 

Bidwell Park marks the latest of several multifamily transactions in the East Bay this year.

title.rendered: Galaxy Commercial ditches hotel for high-rise apartments in Hollywood

content.rendered:
Galaxy Commercial Holdings is pivoting on its development plans for a Sunset Boulevard site in the heart of Hollywood. 

The developer filed an application with the Los Angeles Department of City Planning to develop a 27-story residential high-rise with 239 apartments at 6409 Sunset Boulevard, Urbanize Los Angeles reported. Located on less than an acre site, the building is also slated for 6,000 square feet of ground-floor retail space and parking for 227 vehicles. 

The Galaxy-owned site currently houses a shuttered Jack in the Box fast-food restaurant. The property was previously proposed for an Art Deco hotel tower, but those plans never came to fruition. 

Galaxy Commercial is seeking entitlements, including density bonus incentives, to build a taller structure than zoning rules would normally allow. The developer would provide 37 apartments for rent by very low- and moderate-income tenants to secure the density bonuses. The roughly 300-foot-tall building would come complete with a rooftop amenity deck.

title.rendered: Amendment 3 spells property tax break for homesteads. For renters? Not quite, study says

content.rendered:
As Floridians head to the polls to decide on a property tax amendment, a study found the legislation meant to make homeownership more affordable could burden renters.

Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption on primary homes to $150,000 from the current $50,000 from non-school taxes, with the exemption jumping to $250,000 in 2028. The referendum requires 60 percent of the vote to pass, and if it does, Florida will be the first to implement a statewide property tax overhaul. 

It’s meant to make homeownership more affordable. 

But it makes no mention of apartment tenants, who may be exposed to higher rents if the legislation passes, the Miami Herald reported, citing Washington, D.C.-based Tax Foundation senior fellow and Walczak Policy Consulting President Jared Walczak.

title.rendered: Merchants Bank puts Abraham Leifer’s former Midtown conversion on the market

content.rendered:
Merchants Bank is looking to unload a Midtown apartment building that was caught in a three-year foreclosure battle with troubled landlord Abraham Leifer.

The bank, which took over the 39,000-square-foot building at 19 West 55th Street in July in a foreclosure sale, is eyeing a sale price in the low $20 million range. CBRE’s Dan Kaplan was tapped to market the property.

The vacant nine-story building between Fifth and Sixth avenues was built in 1920. Leifer was planning a conversion to luxury condos when Merchants Bank sued his Aview Equities in March 2023, seeking foreclosure following a string of forbearances.

Merchants alleged in the lawsuit that Leifer failed to repay the balance of a $36.7 million refinance loan, in addition to other defaults including failing to maintain a cash balance of more than $9 million. 

A judgment of foreclosure was issued in July 2024 for about $49 million, plus interest and costs, according to court filings. Two foreclosure sales were postponed after the landlord filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. Both Chapter 11 filings have since been dismissed, said Leifer’s attorney Aaron Slavutin of Jacobs P.C.

title.rendered: Todd Glaser, David Edelstein buying one of Palm Beach’s most-expensive estates for $160M

content.rendered:
Two spec mansion developers are buying one of Palm Beach’s priciest residential properties to tear it down.

Todd Glaser and TriCap’s David Edelstein plan on buying one of Palm Beach’s priciest residential properties for redevelopment.

They are under contract to pay $160 million for 911 North Ocean Boulevard, the Wall Street Journal reported. That’s just under the island’s record, set by luxury car dealer Michael Cantanucci, who paid $170 million for his estate in 2023.

Late developer and philanthropist Murray Goodman and wife, Joanie, listed the property at 911 North Ocean Boulevard for $185 million late last year. The family held the property for more than 50 years, having purchased it for $350,000 in 1974.

The estate has three pink-hued buildings constructed in the mid-1970s totaling about 17,600 square feet, putting the deal at about $9,100 per square foot. It includes a tennis court and 250 feet of ocean frontage on 2.2 acres.

title.rendered: Mill Creek brings multifamily project to fast-growing Pompano Beach

content.rendered:
Mill Creek Residential wants to rezone a chunk of a Pompano Beach car dealership to make way for mixed-income apartments and commercial space. 

MCRT Investments, an affiliate of the Boca Raton-based multifamily development firm, filed an application with the city to rezone a portion of the site at 855-909 South Federal Highway from general business to planned development-infill, according to city documents. 

Pompano Beach’s planning and zoning board will consider the rezoning request Oct. 28. 

Mill Creek plans to redevelop 4.1 acres of the 6.5-acre Gunther Volkswagen Pompano Beach into an eight-story apartment complex called Modera Pompano Beach. 

Plans for Modera call for 347 residential units, 10,400 feet of commercial space and an eight-story garage with 457 parking spaces. Fifty of the units would be designated as affordable housing and reserved for residents making up to 120 percent of the area median income, which is $97,600. The waterfront project would have a courtyard, a pool and a 10,500-square-foot clubhouse, The Real Deal previously reported. 

Property records show Pompano Real Estate Investments LLC, an entity linked to Joseph Accardi of the Joey Accardi Auto Group, owns the property. The entity paid $5.6 million for the property in 2012.

title.rendered: Investor alleges $20M stake in Chicago Loop’s former Citadel Center wiped out by Mike Kohan and his bondraising spree

content.rendered:
An investor who claims he put $19.5 million into the 37-story Chicago office skyscraper at 131 South Dearborn Street is suing Mike Kohan, alleging the embattled landlord wrongly transferred the company controlling the Loop tower to his own firm — a British Virgin Islands vehicle behind his $112 million Israeli bond offering — and wiped out the investor’s stake.

Moise Lavian filed suit late last week in Cook County court against British Virgin Islands-based Kohan Properties Ltd. and Mehran Kohansieh, Kohan’s legal name. Lavian asks the court to declare him the majority owner of 131 South Dearborn Realty Management LLC, the entity atop the ownership chain of the 1.5 million-square-foot former Citadel Center, and accuses Kohansieh of breach of fiduciary duty.

Kohansieh’s group bought the tower in June in a deal worth a little more than $100 million, using a $65 million mortgage from Bayerische Landesbank. The closing paperwork showed Kohansieh owning all of 131 South Dearborn Realty Management LLC, the company at the top of the tower’s ownership chain, according to the suit. Lavian says that changed on July 29, when he signed an updated operating agreement. The agreement listed a 50 percent stake tied to a $12.2 million contribution, but Lavian says he put in more money after that — $19.5 million in all — which made him the majority owner.

title.rendered: Rockrose joins ranks of 421a lawsuit defendants

content.rendered:
Henry Elghanayan is the latest to face a lawsuit alleging rent overcharges tied to the 421a tax program. He has plenty of company.

Tenants at three Long Island City buildings owned by Rockrose Development filed a class-action lawsuit against the developer, QNS reported. The tenants allege their landlord overcharged them by more than $50 million.

The lawsuit centers on three properties: Eagle Lofts, the Linc and Hayden LIC. Residents of the buildings are calling for the overcharges to be refunded and rents to be reset to the net effective base rates originally promised.

The suit follows similar lines to other cases alleging rent overcharges tied to the affordable housing subsidy. Tenants claim the developer was applying increases on rent-stabilized units to the full rent of the apartments and not the preferential rent, which considers concessions such as free months when a lease is initially signed.

The Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 requires rent increases to be applied to preferential rent, not full rent.

title.rendered: E11even developer Marc Roberts fires off anti-Muslim email urging Floridians to protest Islamic centers

content.rendered:
Marc Roberts, a real estate investor behind Miami’s E11even-branded condo towers, is bitterly anti-development when it comes to Islamic centers. 

Roberts recently circulated an email urging recipients to pressure Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis to block Islamic centers, warning that such projects would attract people “violently opposed to our biblical worldview.”

The Oct. 21 mass email, which included a reporter at The Real Deal, targeted purportedly approved religious centers in Delray Beach, West Palm Beach, Loxahatchee and Vero Beach. Roberts called on recipients to contact the governor’s office and their mayors to stop construction.

“Do we want to end up like Dearborn, Michigan, or other states currently governed by individuals holding this ideology?” the message said. “I know I don’t, and I certainly do not want your grandchildren and future generations to live in fear instead of enjoying the freedoms that, by the grace of God, this country has granted us.”

title.rendered: Tishman teams with Dutch investor on office fund

content.rendered:
Rob Speyer has a new office fund underway, a vehicle the Chrysler Building neatly fits into.

Tishman Speyer and Dutch firm Bouwinvest Real Estate Investors launched a joint fund to acquire top office properties throughout the United States, the Commercial Observer reported. Bouwinvest-Tishman Speyer SMA will target both major markets and growth markets.

Details of the fund, including the volume of acquisition targets and the money being earmarked for the fund, were not disclosed. This isn’t the first time the two sides have come together, as the two partnered on a Korea Living Venture fund to invest $400 million in Seoul’s multifamily market.

“Together, we see attractive opportunities to acquire well-located office assets in markets with durable demand drivers and limited new supply, and reposition them to meet the evolving needs of today’s customers,” Tishman executive Nate Shanok said in a statement.

The fund already helped support Tishman’s grand return to the landmark Chrysler Building in Midtown Manhattan.

This month, Tishman and landowner Cooper Union announced a 150-year ground lease for the property. The deal includes a $235 million investment from Tishman and its partners, which include Canada’s PSP Investments.

title.rendered: Mr C Boca developers Wexford and Key seek approval to upsize units

content.rendered:
Wexford Real Estate Investors and Key International are advancing their Mr. C-branded Boca Raton condo after completing a 50 percent pre-sellout.

The developers are seeking city approval to reduce the number of units by 57, increase the size of the building and its parking garage, and secure 6,000 square feet of restaurant space, among other asks that would bring the project’s approval up to speed with the developer’s upscale plans.

Wexford and Key previously planned a 190-unit building before partnering with the Cipriani family’s Mr. C brand. 

The number of planned units were cut to 133 — a request the city’s Community Redevelopment Agency is set to vote on today. Two other city committees already gave unanimous approval.

The developers bought the property for $25.5 million in 2023 and announced the partnership with Mr. C in January. Key International is led by Inigo and Diego Ardid, and Wexford is led by president Joseph M. Jacobs and managing principal Philip Braunstein.

title.rendered: Caught in the syndicator spiral: The worst apartments in the nucleus of the multifamily frenzy

content.rendered:
North Texas’ worst apartment complexes have more in common than the fact that they’ve all been sitting empty, having recently been evacuated after years of code compliance issues. 

They’re all owned by multifamily syndicators.

These investors pitched their firms as value-add operations, raising pooled capital for plans to buy and revamp outdated apartment complexes, then sell them at a profit. They tore through Sun Belt growth spots like Dallas-Fort Worth in the early 2020s until rising interest rates flipped on the lights at the party. 

Now, in the worst-of-the-worst examples of the syndicator spiral, a handful of North Texas properties are vacant after municipalities turned to legal intervention — a rare path in the landlord-friendly state.

title.rendered: Jupiter waterfront mansion designed for Céline Dion trades for $13M

content.rendered:
A waterfront mansion in Jupiter built in the 1990s for singer Céline Dion traded hands for $12.5 million.

Local investor Myron Miller bought the house at 370 Eagle Drive for $847 per square foot. The seller was an entity registered to Edward St. John, founder of Baltimore-based St. John Properties.

The deal was done off-market, though it was offered at $20 million in June, according to a post by seller’s agent Rob Thomson of Waterfront Properties. The house last sold for $7.6 million in 2021, meaning its price increased 64 percent over five years.

The 14,750-square-foot home sits on a 0.66-acre lot and has eight bedrooms, eight bathrooms, and three half-baths, along with a theater, pool and private dock. It’s in the gated Admirals Cove neighborhood, home to a country club with a golf course and water access.

Thomson noted there’s “no chance” the 1998 home built for Dion would be torn down, and that the neighborhood’s comprehensive amenities makes it like a “Disney for adults.”

The buyer is an avid golfer, which made the neighborhood a good fit, said buyer’s agent Willie Abreu of Serhant’s The Nicolas Group. Jupiter’s housing market is strong, he added, as ultra-wealthy buyers look for hideaways that are still near business hubs in West Palm Beach and Miami.
